title: Adjectives and adverbs 1 (quick/quickly)
subtitle: quick / quickly
summary: Use adjectives (quick, careful) to describe nouns and adverbs (quickly, carefully) to describe how something happens, and use adverbs before adjectives and past participles.

lesson.heading: Adverbs: adjective + -ly
lesson.text: **Quickly** and **seriously** are adverbs. Many adverbs are adjective + **-ly**: quick → quickly, serious → seriously, careful → carefully, bad → badly, heavy → heavily, terrible → terribly.

examples.text: Our holiday was too short - the time passed very **quickly**.
Two people were **seriously** injured in the accident.

lesson.heading: Not every -ly word is an adverb
lesson.text: Some adjectives end in **-ly** too, for example **friendly, lively, elderly, lonely, lovely**. They describe nouns, not verbs.

left.label: Adjectives tell us about a noun
left.text: We use adjectives before nouns (somebody or something).
examples: Sam is a **careful** driver. (not a carefully driver)
We didn't go out because of the **heavy** rain.

right.label: Adverbs tell us about a verb
right.text: Adverbs say how somebody does something or how something happens.
examples: Sam drove **carefully** along the narrow road. (not drove careful)
We didn't go out because it was raining **heavily**. (not raining heavy)

left.label: Adjective after be/look/feel/sound
examples: Why do you always look so **serious**?

right.label: Adverb with other verbs
examples: I did really **badly** in the exam.
Why do you never take me **seriously**?

lesson.heading: Adverb + adjective, adverb + adverb
lesson.text: You can also use adverbs before adjectives and other adverbs: **reasonably** cheap, **terribly** sorry, **incredibly** quickly. You can also use an adverb before a past participle (injured/organised/written etc.).

examples.text: It's a **reasonably cheap** restaurant and the food is **extremely good**.
I'm **terribly sorry**. I didn't mean to push you.
Maria learns languages **incredibly quickly**. The exam was **surprisingly easy**.
Two people were **seriously injured** in the accident.

lesson.text: If the word describes a person or thing (a noun), use the adjective. If it answers 'how?' about an action, or comes before another adjective, use the adverb.

exercises.prompt: I had no problem finding a place to live. I found a flat quite ___.
exercises.explanation: The word says how I found the flat, so we need the adverb: easily.

exercises.prompt: We had to wait a long time, but we didn't complain. We waited ___.
exercises.explanation: How did we wait? Patiently - an adverb describing the verb.

exercises.prompt: The weather changed ___. There was a ___ change in the weather.
exercises.explanation: The adverb suddenly describes the verb changed; the adjective sudden describes the noun change.

exercises.statement: I think I have flu. I feel awfully.
exercises.explanation: I feel awful. After feel we use an adjective, not an adverb.

exercises.prompt: Nobody knew that Simon was coming to see us. He arrived ___.
exercises.explanation: The adverb unexpectedly tells us how he arrived.

exercises.prompt: Does the gap need the adjective or the adverb?

items.text: I think you behaved very ___. (selfish / selfishly)
I could sit in this chair all day. It's very ___. (comfortable / comfortably)
I explained everything as ___ as I could. (clear / clearly)
Tanya is ___ upset about losing her job. (terrible / terribly)
Be careful on that ladder. It doesn't look very ___. (safe / safely)
Have a good trip and I hope you have a ___ journey. (safe / safely)

exercises.prompt: Maria's English is very ___ although she makes quite a lot of mistakes.
exercises.explanation: After is we use an adjective to describe her English: fluent.

exercises.prompt: I cooked this meal ___ for you, so I hope you like it.
exercises.explanation: The adverb specially says how (for what purpose) I cooked the meal.

exercises.prompt: Be careful on that ladder. It doesn't look very ___. I'm glad you got home ___.
exercises.explanation: After look we use the adjective safe; got home safely uses the adverb to say how you got home.

exercises.statement: Liz fell and hurt herself really bad.
exercises.explanation: Liz fell and hurt herself really badly. The adverb badly describes how she hurt herself.

exercises.prompt: Match each sentence with the adverb + adjective that completes it.

pairs.left: This house is so big! It's ...
It wasn't a serious accident. The car was only ...
Our children are normally very lively, but they're ... today.
When I returned home after 20 years, everything had ...
The movie was ... It could have been much shorter.

exercises.prompt: Dan likes to take risks. He lives ___.
exercises.explanation: How does he live? Dangerously - an adverb after the verb lives.
